WHAT NOBODY TELLS YOU BEFORE YOU FLY TO VIETNAM. SO HERE I AM.
vietnam is easy once you know the small rules, but the first 24 hours can get expensive fast if you make decisions on autopilot. these are the things i'd have sorted before my plane even lands.

THE FIRST APP YOU SHOULD OPEN ISN'T INSTAGRAM.
it's grab. download it and register it before you land, not after, because the mistake people make is trying to set it up for the first time standing at arrivals with bags in both hands and a driver already offering to "help." 
2
/
9
1
1

AND STOP FLAGGING DOWN STREET TAXIS OUT OF HABIT.
grab locks the price before you get in, no negotiating, no meter to watch. if you do need a street taxi, mai linh (green) or vinasun (white and red) are the two names actually worth trusting. 
3
/
9
1

YOUR EXCHANGE RATE MATH ALSO NEEDS TO BE AUTOMATIC.
1 usd is about 26,000 dong, and that's exactly why the extra zero trick works. a price written as 20,000 and one written as 200,000 are one digit apart on a menu and a real amount of money apart in your pocket, easy to misread when you're jet lagged and the numbers still feel unfamiliar. know the number cold before you land, not after you've paid it. 
4
/
9
1
1

THEN THERE'S THE AIRPORT SIM COUNTER.
it's 20 to 30% more than the exact same plan sold at a shop in the city. if you can hold out an hour before buying, do. and if you're taking grab into the city, expect roughly 130,000 to 390,000 dong depending on distance. 
5
/
9
1

DO NOT BUILD YOUR VIETNAM BUDGET AROUND HOTEL BREAKFAST PRICES.
a comfortable planning benchmark in the guide is around 40 dollars a day, covering food, local transport, one paid activity and a small buffer. that's a completely different number than treating every meal like a special occasion. 
6
/
9
1

YOUR CHEAPEST MEALS CAN ALSO BE THE BEST ONES IN THE COUNTRY.
a real bowl of pho, bun cha off the beaten path, banh mi from a stall with a line out front. none of that is backpacker mode, it's just knowing where the good version of something actually is.

9
1
1

AND BEFORE YOU LEAVE HOME, CHECK WHETHER YOU EVEN NEED A VISA.
a growing list of countries enter visa free for up to 45 days. everyone else needs the e-visa, 25 dollars direct through the official site, not a third party site charging 50 to 80 for the same thing. solve this before takeoff, not at immigration.

1. Grab and Xanh SM, both downloaded and registered with a working number. Trying to set this up for the first time at arrivals with bags in both hands is how people end up in someone else's car instead.
2. An eSIM installed before takeoff, or you're stuck paying the airport counter markup for the first hour on the ground. 
2
/
7
1
1

3. Cash withdrawn for day one, from a bank that doesn't sting you with a foreign card fee. Not all of them do.
4. Your first night's hotel address, saved offline, ideally in Vietnamese. Most drivers don't read an English address off your phone. 
3
/
7
1

5. The current dong to dollar rate, roughly 26,000 to 1, memorized well enough that you're not doing the math slowly while someone's waiting on an answer.
6. A rough idea of what a normal day should cost you, so a quote either matches what you expected or doesn't. 
4
/
7
1

7. Your visa status confirmed, not assumed. Some passports are visa free up to 45 days, others need the e-visa, and the list of which is which changed again last year.
8. A passport copy saved offline, in case the physical one goes missing for a day. 
5
/
7
1
1

9. Something to cover shoulders and knees for the first temple you'll inevitably end up walking past and wanting to go inside.
10. Small notes on hand before you need them. Nobody's breaking a big bill for a bottle of water at 7am. 
6

7
1

None of these take more than ten minutes total. All ten take considerably longer to fix once you're already standing there needing them.

CHEAPER THAN YOU'D THINK
1. A short Grab ride across town. Often under a dollar.
2. A proper bowl of pho at a local spot, not a hotel menu.
3. Vietnamese coffee, including the egg coffee everyone posts about. 
2
/
7
4
1

4. A tailor made outfit in Hoi An, genuinely cheaper than most people expect walking in.
5. A sleeper train berth between major cities, once you compare it to a flight plus a hotel night.
6. Fresh fruit and street snacks, priced in cents rather than dollars almost everywhere outside a tourist strip. 
3
/
7
4
1

PRICIER THAN YOU'D THINK
1. Entry to a handful of major sites, like Hue's Imperial City, which busts the usual daily activity budget on its own.
2. Domestic flights booked less than two weeks out. 
4
/
7
3
1

3. A menu with English and photos parked right next to a major landmark. The markup is built into the location, not the food.
4. Third party e-visa websites charging double or triple the official government fee for the same visa. 
5
/
7
3
1

5. Anything during the week of Tet, when prices on rooms and transport commonly double.
6. A "government" gem or jewelry stop a friendly local walks you toward. Never government, rarely a good price. 
6

1

The pattern isn't that Vietnam is cheap or expensive. It's that the gap between the two lists is exactly where people either save or lose money without realizing which one they're standing in.

threads.title: 6 THINGS TO EAT IN VIETNAM THAT AREN'T PHO, AND MOST FIRST TIMERS NEVER TRY A SINGLE ONE.

parts.text:
6 THINGS TO EAT IN VIETNAM THAT AREN'T PHO, AND MOST FIRST TIMERS NEVER TRY A SINGLE ONE. 
1
/
9
5
9
1
Top
View activity




Reply to vietnamcontext...

1. Bun cha, grilled pork with noodles. Charred pork patties and pork belly in a sweet and sour broth, served with cold rice noodles and a pile of herbs on the side. The Hanoi dish that put the whole country on an American president's radar years ago. A bowl runs around 60,000 dong ($2.30). 
2
/
9
4
1
1

2. Banh xeo, the crispy rice pancake. Turmeric batter, shrimp, pork, and bean sprouts folded into a big crackling pancake, torn apart and wrapped in lettuce and herbs before you eat it. More popular in the south and central regions than most tourists ever hear about. Typically 40,000 to 70,000 dong ($1.50 to $2.70). 
3
/
9
1
1

3. Cao lau, the noodle you can only get in Hoi An. Thick, chewy noodles, said to be made with water from one specific local well, topped with pork and crunchy croutons. It genuinely doesn't exist properly outside that one town. A bowl runs about 30,000 to 50,000 dong ($1.15 to $1.90). 
4
/
9
1

4. Banh mi, but the version worth lining up for. Not the hotel lobby version, the stall with a line of locals and a single grill going since sunrise. Crackling baguette, pate, cold cuts, pickled vegetables, done in under a minute. A proper one runs 20,000 to 45,000 dong ($0.75 to $1.75). 
5
/
9
1

5. Bun bo Hue, spicy beef and pork noodle soup. Lemongrass and chili oil in a broth that's got real heat to it, a completely different animal from a bowl of pho. Mornings only at most of the best spots, gone by mid day. Usually 30,000 to 40,000 dong ($1.15 to $1.55). 
6
/
9
1
1

6. Egg coffee, ca phe trung. Whipped egg yolk and condensed milk poured over strong Vietnamese coffee, invented in Hanoi in the 1940s during a milk shortage and never stopped being ordered since. Around 35,000 to 45,000 dong ($1.35 to $1.70) at the place where it started. 
7
/
9
1
1

Pho isn't a bad dish. It's just the one dish every menu outside the country already knows how to make for a foreign crowd, which is exactly why it's rarely the best version of anything once you're actually there. The six above are what gets ordered on a normal Tuesday. 
8
/
9
1

There's a flower market on the edge of Hanoi that runs almost entirely while the rest of the city is asleep.
Quang An, right by Nhat Tan Bridge along the West Lake, gets its deliveries from villages outside the city starting around three in the morning.

By four it's a full working market, buckets of peonies and lotus and whatever's in season stacked shoulder high, vendors calling out prices, motorbikes weaving through with flowers strapped on in every direction. It's not styled for tourists at all.

It exists because Hanoi buys an enormous amount of fresh flowers daily for temples, weddings, and just decorating homes, and this is where that entire supply chain starts.

Most visitors never see it because it's essentially over by sunrise, back to a normal quiet riverside spot by the time regular breakfast crowds are out. If you're jet lagged anyway in your first couple days, this is the version of "up early in Hanoi" that actually pays off, and it's a completely different image of the city than the Old Quarter gives you.

The driver accepted the booking, then took her phone and cancelled the trip himself without asking her, which already should have been the first red flag. He kept driving her to the destination anyway. When they arrived he demanded more than double the original price in cash.

She refused, he pushed back, and the whole argument got filmed by someone nearby and ended up all over Vietnamese Threads and Facebook within a day. Authorities in the district ended up opening an investigation because the clip had gone so viral it was actually becoming a talking point about how Hanoi looks to visitors.

Here's the part that matters for you. The scam only worked because the driver cancelled the trip in the app first. Once a ride is cancelled you have no fare protection, no record, nothing to point to.
